title: Problem 1.1 (Erdős)
statement_text: Let $k\geq 4$. For every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ let $f_{k}(n)$ denote the largest integer $r\geq 1$ such that there exists a $(k,r)$-graph on $n$ vertices ($f_{k}(n):=0$ if no such graph exists for any $r\geq 1$). Is it true that $f_{k}(n)\rightarrow\infty$ for $n\rightarrow\infty$?
context_text: Erdős posed this in 1985 as a strong version of Dirac's conjecture, asking whether for every $k\geq 4$ and $r\geq 1$ there exists a $k$-vertex-critical graph in which no set of at most $r$ edges is critical. The case $r=1$ corresponds to Dirac's conjecture. The problem has been reiterated in several books and problem collections (cf. page 66 of [3] and [4, 7]).
paper_contribution: Solves the problem affirmatively for all $k\geq 5$, proving $f_k(n)=\Omega(n^{1/3})$; the case $k=4$ remains open.
paper_title: Critical edge sets in vertex-critical graphs

title: Problem 5.2
context_text: A vertex, edge or set of edges of a graph $G$ is critical if its removal yields a graph with smaller chromatic number than $G$; a graph $G$ with $\chi(G)=k$ is $k$-vertex-critical if every vertex is critical. A $(k,r)$-graph is a $k$-vertex-critical graph in which no set of at most $r$ edges is critical; so a $(4,1)$-graph is a 4-vertex-critical graph with no critical edge, i.e. removing any single edge leaves a graph that is still not 3-colorable. Dirac conjectured in 1970 that $(k,1)$-graphs exist for every $k\ge4$, and Erdős (1985) asked whether $(k,r)$-graphs exist for all $k\ge4$ and $r\ge1$. The authors prove that $(k,r)$-graphs exist for all $k\ge5$ and $r\ge1$ (with order $n$ and $r=\Omega(n^{1/3})$), so the only remaining open case of both Dirac's and Erdős's problems is $k=4$; in particular it is open whether a $(4,1)$-graph exists at all. Their circulant constructions cannot settle $k=4$, and they lean towards thinking that no circulant $(4,1)$-graph exists. They prove that every $(4,r)$-graph has edge-connectivity, hence minimum degree, at least $3r+3$ and maximum degree at most $|V(G)|-(2r+3)$; thus a $(4,1)$-graph has minimum degree at least $6$, and the sparsest option left is a 6-regular graph, which makes the search for 6-regular examples natural from a computational viewpoint.
paper_title: Critical edge sets in vertex-critical graphs
